lead: Today's two readings belong together: both speak of priests. Hebrews says that no one takes the priestly office for himself; he is called by God, “just as Aaron was”. Luke opens his Gospel inside the temple, with a priest named Zechariah, his wife Elizabeth, who is “a descendant of Aaron”, and a whole people praying outside while the incense burns. The Panchangam remembers Aaron on this first day of July, and the readings show what a priest is: someone called, set apart to offer gifts and sacrifices on behalf of the people, and himself in need of mercy. The key words are called and righteous.

r.h: Called by God, just as Aaron was
set: The Letter to the Hebrews is a long sermon, written by an author the Church does not name. It was received early as part of the Pauline tradition, though almost all scholars agree that its style and thought differ from Paul's; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture. It is addressed to Christians of Jewish background who were tempted to lose heart, and it shows that everything good in the worship of Israel finds its fulfilment in Christ.

Chapter 4 ended by calling Jesus the great high priest who has passed through the heavens and can sympathise with our weakness (4:14–16). Chapter 5 now explains what any high priest is, so that the author can show how Jesus is one, and more than one (5:5–10). Today's four verses are a portrait of the high priest of Israel, of whom Aaron, the brother of Moses, was the first.
str: v. 1: the high priest is taken from among human beings and appointed to act for them before God, offering gifts and sacrifices for sins.
vv. 2–3: he can be gentle with the ignorant and the wayward because he shares their weakness, and so he offers also for his own sins.
v. 4: no one takes the honour for himself; he is called by God, as Aaron was.
¶ Three marks of a priest: he is one of us, he stands before God for us, and he is called.
kw: A rare Greek verb, meaning to bear with feelings that are measured and gentle, neither hard nor careless. The priest can be patient with sinners because he knows his own weakness. The same letter says of Jesus that he “has been tested as we are, yet without sin” (4:15).
Priesthood is not a career chosen from within; it is a vocation received from outside. In the Old Testament God summoned Aaron and his sons (Exodus 28:1).
A pair of words for all that Israel offered: grain and first-fruits on one side, animals on the other. The priest carries the offerings of the people to God.
vv: Every high priest chosen from among mortals is put in charge of things pertaining to God on their behalf, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.
A priest does not stand above the people; he is “chosen from among mortals”. He is one of them, and he is appointed for them.
He is able to deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, since he himself is subject to weakness;
The priest's own weakness is meant to make him merciful, not harsh. A priest who forgets that he is a sinner forgets his work.
and because of this he must offer sacrifice for his own sins as well as for those of the people.

On the Day of Atonement Aaron had first to offer a bull for himself and his household, and only then the goat for the people (Leviticus 16:6, 11, 15). This is the very point where Jesus differs: he has no sin of his own to atone for (Hebrews 7:27).
And one does not presume to take this honor, but takes it only when called by God, just as Aaron was.
Aaron did not seek the office; God chose him and his sons, and Moses consecrated them (Exodus 28–29). The call comes first, and the ordination confirms it.
ch: The Catechism begins its teaching on the priesthood with the Old Testament: God made Israel a priestly kingdom (Exodus 19:6), set apart the tribe of Levi for the liturgy, and appointed priests to act for the people before God and to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, recalling this very verse (CCC 1539). All that the priesthood of the old covenant prefigured is fulfilled in Christ, the one mediator between God and human beings (CCC 1544). The Church also applies verse 4 to every vocation to Holy Orders: no one has a right to ordination, and no one claims the office for himself; he is called by God (CCC 1578).

r.h: A priest, his wife and the praying people
set: Luke begins his Gospel with a short preface (1:1–4) and then, at once, goes to Jerusalem. The first scene is not in Bethlehem or Nazareth but in the temple, at the hour of the incense offering. The Gospel will end in the same place: after the Ascension the disciples “were continually in the temple blessing God” (24:53).

The priests of Israel were divided into twenty-four sections, which served in the temple in turn for a week at a time (1 Chronicles 24:1–19); the section of Abijah was the eighth (24:10). Zechariah was a priest of that section. The time is “the days of King Herod”, so the story is set before Herod's death, about 4 BC. Zechariah and Elizabeth are the opening figures of the new beginning that God is about to make.
str: vv. 5–7: the couple: a priest of the section of Abijah and his wife, a descendant of Aaron; both righteous and without children.
vv. 8–9: Zechariah is chosen by lot to enter the sanctuary and offer incense.
v. 10: the whole assembly is praying outside.
¶ The story continues after today's verses with the angel at the altar of incense (1:11–20).
kw: Right with God. The word is used of Joseph (Matthew 1:19) and of Simeon (Luke 2:25). Luke wants us to see that the Saviour is born into a world where faithful people have been waiting.
Without reproach. It does not mean sinless, but wholehearted in keeping “all the commandments and regulations of the Lord”.

The incense offered morning and evening on the golden altar before the veil of the sanctuary (Exodus 30:7–8). Its rising smoke is, in Scripture, the picture of prayer going up to God (Psalm 141:2; Revelation 8:3–4).
vv: His wife was a descendant of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth.
Elizabeth is from the priestly family of Aaron, the very man whom the Epistle recalls today. In Hebrew her name is Elisheba, the name of Aaron's own wife (Exodus 6:23).
Both of them were righteous before God, living blamelessly according to all the commandments and regulations of the Lord.
Luke honours the faith of Israel. The new covenant does not begin by despising the old; it begins with two faithful servants of the Law.
But they had no children, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were getting on in years.
Like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Hannah before her, Elizabeth is childless. In Scripture, whenever God gives a child to such a woman, he is about to do something new.
he was chosen by lot, according to the custom of the priesthood, to enter the sanctuary of the Lord and offer incense.

The lot was cast, and according to later Jewish tradition a priest might receive this honour only once in his life. God's choice comes through what looks like chance, as it did when Matthias was chosen (Acts 1:26).
Now at the time of the incense offering, the whole assembly of the people was praying outside.
The people do not watch; they pray. The first sound of the New Testament is the prayer of the people of God, joined to the offering of the priest.
ch: The Church sees in Zechariah and Elizabeth the last of the righteous of the old covenant, and in the birth of their son John the end of the long waiting: the Catechism says that John surpasses all the prophets, of whom he is the last, and is the immediate forerunner of the Lord (CCC 523). The Church also sees in the incense and the praying assembly the pattern of her own worship, where the priest offers and the people pray with him. The Syriac tradition, with its great use of incense in the Qurbono, has always loved this picture.

qa: Why does Hebrews say that a priest must offer sacrifice for his own sins?

Because every priest of the old covenant was a sinner. On the Day of Atonement Aaron had to bring a sin offering for himself before he could offer for the people (Leviticus 16:6). The author uses this to show what is new in Jesus: he is the priest who needs no offering for himself, because he is without sin (Hebrews 4:15; 7:27). A priest of the Church today, who is a sinner, still comes to confession and prays humbly at every Qurbono, and he does so because his priesthood is a sharing in the priesthood of Christ, not a power of his own.
rite: The Panchangam remembers Aaron the High Priest today, on the first day of July, which the Syriac calendar calls Tammuz. The memory is a reminder that the priesthood by which the Holy Qurbono is celebrated has its roots in the call of Aaron, and is fulfilled in Christ, the one High Priest. The Malankara faithful pray for their bishops and priests at every Qurbono; today's readings invite them to pray that those who are called will be faithful, gentle and merciful.
study: The high priest is “chosen from among mortals” and can be gentle because he knows his own weakness. How can I be patient with someone else's failings, remembering my own?
Zechariah and Elizabeth were righteous, yet childless and old. What waiting in my life is God asking me to bring to prayer?
The people were praying outside while the priest offered incense. How do I take part in the prayer of the Church at the Holy Qurbono, and not only watch?
